name: Squat

lead: The squat lowers the hips from standing and drives back up. It trains the quadriceps, glutes, adductors and trunk and is one of the three powerlifting lifts, alongside the bench press and deadlift.[1]
For looks, it is the basis for leg size, glute development and overall muscle mass. Training communities often treat it as a foundation lift in programmes for building a fuller physique.

paras: People squat with a barbell on the back or front, with dumbbells, a machine or bodyweight, usually as part of a weekly programme with other lifts. Variations such as front, goblet, split and hack squats shift emphasis between muscles.

Common concerns are lower-back and knee strain, linked to poor form, excess load or rapid descent. A 2013 review found deep squats with proper technique did not raise degenerative knee injury rates.[1] Equipment such as safety bars and power cages is used for support.

chain: Loaded squatting trains quads, glutes and trunk
Larger, stronger legs and a fuller physique
angle.text: People squat to build leg and glute size and overall muscle mass. A 10-week trial found that full-depth squat training grew most thigh muscles by more than half-depth squatting did, and barbell, dumbbell and bodyweight versions let the lift fit many training setups.[4]

lead: The squat is a strength exercise in which the trainee lowers the hips by bending the hips and knees, then stands back up. The main movers are the quadriceps, gluteus maximus and adductor magnus, with the spinal erectors, abdominals, obliques and calves working to stabilise.[1] It is one of the three lifts contested in powerlifting, alongside the bench press and deadlift.[2]

For appearance, the squat is used to add size to the thighs and glutes and to build overall muscle mass, since a heavy, multi-joint lift lets a trainee load a large amount of muscle at once. Lifters use barbell back and front squats, dumbbell or kettlebell goblet squats, machines, single-leg variations and bodyweight squats, and the exercise sits at the centre of many strength and hypertrophy programmes.[1]

Research on the lift covers muscle activation, the effect of squat depth on thigh muscle growth, the biomechanics of the movement, its use in rehabilitation, and how training variables such as rest periods and proximity to failure affect strength and muscle size in lifters who squat.[3][4][5][6][7] On looksmax.org, squat numbers are a common reference point in discussions of lifting and physique.[8][9]
infobox: Hip crease below the top of the knee (IPF)[2]
Back, front, goblet, split, hack, Zercher
Barbell, power cage, belt, safety squat bar, machines
First lift in a powerlifting meet[2]

paras: In a standard barbell back squat the bar rests across the upper back, the lifter walks it out of a rack, descends by flexing the hips, knees and ankles, and drives upward to standing. High-bar and low-bar positions shift the bar's placement on the back and change how much the torso leans.[1]

Depth is debated. Powerlifting's competition standard is that the hip crease passes below the top of the knee, informally called parallel; some federations accept hip joint parallel with the knee.[1][2] Commonly listed technique errors are descending too quickly, leaning the torso too far forward, the knees collapsing inward and the heels lifting.[1]
Common equipment includes power cages, Smith machines, lifting belts, wrist straps and safety squat bars, while chains and bands are used to vary resistance through the range of motion.[1]

Barbell variations include the back squat, front squat, overhead squat, Zercher squat and Steinborn squat. Other forms include the hack squat, goblet squat, belt squat, trap-bar squat, split and Bulgarian split squat, pistol squat, shrimp squat and sissy squat.[1]

Bodyweight forms include the air squat and the Hindu squat (baithak), which was a staple of traditional Indian wrestlers and is associated with wrestler The Great Gama and with Bruce Lee's training.[1] Different variations shift emphasis between the quadriceps, glutes and adductors and suit different equipment and mobility.[1]

Squatting is old as a training movement, and several variants carry the names of early strength athletes: George Hackenschmidt popularised the hack squat in English-speaking countries in the early 1900s, the Zercher squat is named after 1930s strongman Ed Zercher, and the Steinborn squat after strongman Henry "Milo" Steinborn.[1]

As a competition lift, the squat entered organised powerlifting, which emerged in the UK and US in the 1950s from the older "odd lifts" tradition. The International Powerlifting Federation was formed in November 1972, with its first World Championships in 1973; women's competition was added by the IPF in 1980.[2] Raw, unequipped lifting has grown rapidly since the late 2000s.[2]

In a standard meet the squat is performed first, and the lifter waits for the head referee's signal before racking the bar. Typical disqualifying faults include failing to reach depth, double bouncing, and not standing fully erect.[2] Federations differ on equipment, drug testing and depth interpretation.[2]

Wikipedia lists selected records of 595 kg for the equipped men's squat (Nathan Baptist, 2021) and 421.5 kg for a raw men's squat without wraps or sleeves (Paul Anderson, 1965); women's records include 432.5 kg equipped (Leah Reichman, 2023) and 320 kg raw with sleeves (Sonita Muluh, 2025).[1]

A 2020 systematic review of 16 studies measured gluteus maximus activation during loaded hip-extension exercises. Exercises with very high activation (above 60 percent of maximal voluntary isometric contraction) included the step-up and its variations, hip thrust variants, deadlifts, lunges, the split squat and the belt squat; step-ups showed the highest levels.[3]

A 2019 trial in the European Journal of Applied Physiology randomised 17 men to full or half squat training twice weekly for 10 weeks and measured thigh muscle volume by MRI. Knee extensor volume rose 4.9 percent in the full-squat group, and the authors concluded full squats were more effective for developing the lower-limb muscles apart from the rectus femoris and hamstrings.[4]

A 2016 randomised trial of 21 resistance-trained men compared 1-minute with 3-minute rests across eight weeks of whole-body training that included back squats. Squat strength and anterior-thigh muscle thickness were greater in the 3-minute group.[5] A 2023 trial in resistance-trained adults used squat, bench and deadlift for five weeks and compared training near failure with stopping four to six repetitions short, reporting that strength gains did not differ significantly between groups.[6]

Commonly reported problems are lower-back and knee strain, associated with poor form, excessive load or rapid descent.[1] A 2013 review (Hartmann and colleagues, summarised on Wikipedia) concluded that deep squats performed with proper technique did not increase rates of degenerative knee injury.[1]

A 2023 JAMA review of knee pain notes that anterior knee pain during a squat is about 91 percent sensitive, and 50 percent specific, for patellofemoral pain, which has a lifetime prevalence of about 25 percent in physically active people under 40.[7] On looksmax.org, one member described lower-back pain after attempting a heavy squat.[8]

Squat variants are used clinically. A 2024 biomechanical review summarises the mechanics of the squat for clinical practice,[9] and Wikipedia notes decline squats are used in rehabilitation.[1] In a 2009 randomised trial of 39 men with patellar tendinopathy, eccentric decline squat training, heavy slow resistance training and corticosteroid injections all improved symptoms at 12 weeks; improvements were maintained at six months with the exercise approaches but not the injections.[10]

A looksmax.org thread discusses the idea, attributed there to coach Jason Blaha, that reaching a set squat strength standard produces a muscular physique; the original poster argues volume builds size and that strength-standard programmes can sacrifice size in some muscles.[11] Another member reported adding load on squat and overhead press during the third week of a testosterone regimen.[12]
A third thread asks what the squat equivalent would be in a hunter-gatherer setting; replies point to the bodyweight squat and to walking and running as sources of leg strength.[13]

Human studies have examined gluteal muscle activation across loaded exercises,[3] full versus half squat depth and thigh muscle volume,[4] rest-interval effects on squat strength and muscle thickness,[5] training proximity to failure,[6] and squat-based rehabilitation for patellar tendinopathy.[10] A 2023 meta-analysis of 270 trials also reported that dynamic resistance training lowered resting blood pressure by about 4.55/3.04 mm Hg.[14]

lore.intro: Squat strength is a frequent reference point in lifting discussion on looksmax.org, from strength-standard philosophies to training logs.[11][12]
